opus-5.5.text:
I think the framing of privacy versus utility is partly real and partly a false choice, and good design should take both of those seriously.

The real part is that health is about the most context-dependent domain there is. The answer to "is this headache worth worrying about?" depends a lot on your history, your medications, your recent labs, what's going on in your life. So the more relevant context a model has, the more useful and safer its answer tends to be. People sense that, and they also sense that sharing that context carries risk. That instinct is reasonable.

The false-choice part is the assumption that getting utility means giving up control. A lot of the design work is about breaking that link. A few principles I'd emphasize:

First, separation. Health conversations and connected records should live in their own protected space, with stronger safeguards, and shouldn't spill into the rest of your experience or be used to train models by default. People should know that what they share about a diagnosis stays scoped to that purpose.

Second, user control that's actually legible. Not a forty-page policy, but clear choices: what's connected, what's remembered, and an easy way to see it, change it, or delete it. If people feel they can pull data back out, they're more willing to share it in the first place, and that's where the utility comes from.

Third, minimization by default. The system should pull in the context that's relevant to the question rather than everything it can reach. That's better for privacy, and honestly often better for answer quality too, because irrelevant context can distract.

Fourth, earning trust over time rather than demanding it upfront. Someone might start by asking general questions with no personal data, see that the answers are careful and useful, and then choose to connect more. The product should work well at every level of sharing, not punish people who share less.

The underlying point is that trust is itself a precondition for utility in health. If people don't trust the system, they withhold information or don't use it at all, and then it can't help them. So investing heavily in privacy isn't a tax on usefulness. In this domain it's part of what makes usefulness possible.

r001.rationale: It says health conversations and connected records should not be used to train models by default, and that clear control makes people more willing to share health data.

r002.rationale: It describes the value of relevant personal health context but does not say ChatGPT Health can benefit from a user's context elsewhere in ChatGPT.

r003.rationale: It says health conversations and connected records should not spill into the rest of the user's experience.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that the tension is real, and I don't want to wave it away. People are being asked to share some of the most sensitive information about themselves, and in exchange they're hoping to get something genuinely useful back. If you ask most people in the abstract, "do you want more privacy or more utility," they'll say privacy. But if you watch what they actually do, they'll often share quite a lot when they believe it's going to help them. So part of what we're trying to design for is that gap between the stated preference and the revealed preference, and to make sure people never feel like they got tricked by it.

The way I think about it is that privacy and utility aren't really opposites; they're more like two constraints you have to satisfy at the same time. The failure mode is treating privacy as a tax you pay on utility, where every protection you add makes the product worse. We've tried pretty hard to avoid that framing. For example, health conversations in ChatGPT are kept separate from the rest of your experience. That's a privacy decision, but it's also a utility decision, because it means the model isn't dragging in context from your work or your personal life that has nothing to do with your health. The separation actually makes the health experience better.

The second principle is that control has to be real and legible, not buried. If you connect your medical records or a wearable, you should be able to see exactly what's connected, and disconnect it in one step, and have that actually mean something. A lot of health products historically have had privacy policies that are technically disclosed and practically invisible. I don't think that's good enough, especially when the thing on the other end is a model that can reason about your data in ways that a dashboard never could. The more capable the system, the more the user needs to understand what it knows and why.

Third, we've been very deliberate about what the data is not used for. Health conversations aren't used to train our foundation models. That's not just a policy line for us; it changes the risk calculus for the person deciding whether to share. If someone is worried that describing a symptom is going to end up somewhere they didn't anticipate, that worry is a utility problem too, because they'll hold back, and then the model can't help them well. So the privacy commitment is, in a sense, what unlocks the utility.

And then I'd say the last piece is honesty about limits. We're not a substitute for a clinician, and we try to be clear about that, especially around diagnosis and treatment. Part of respecting people's privacy is respecting their judgment: giving them enough context to decide for themselves what to share, what to ask, and when to take something to a doctor. If you get that right, I think the perceived tension starts to dissolve a bit, because people can see that the system is designed to work for them rather than extract from them.

r001.rationale: The response says health conversations are not used to train foundation models and explains that this reassurance can reduce users’ hesitation to share, allowing the model to help them.

r002.rationale: It says context from work or personal life is not dragged into the health experience, but does not state that ChatGPT Health can benefit from context elsewhere in ChatGPT.

r003.rationale: It describes health conversations as separate from the rest of the experience, but does not clearly state that conversations outside ChatGPT Health do not receive health context.

astra-6.text:
I think the goal should be to make that tradeoff as small as possible, rather than asking people to choose between privacy and something useful. Health is a place where context can really matter, but it’s also a place where people understandably want a lot of control over what they share.

So I’d start with clear boundaries: What information am I giving the system? What will it be used for? How long does it stay available? And can I remove it? Those should be things you can understand and control without having to become a privacy expert.

Then sharing more context should be a deliberate choice, with a clear benefit. If you can get a useful answer without connecting additional information, great. If additional context would help, the product should explain why and let you decide. I think trust comes from making those choices meaningful and making the system’s behavior match what people reasonably expect.

r001.rationale: The response discusses privacy choices and control, but does not mention excluding ChatGPT Health data from foundation-model training or lowering the barrier to use.

r002.rationale: It says additional context may improve an answer, but does not state that ChatGPT Health can benefit from a user's context elsewhere in ChatGPT.

r003.rationale: It does not address whether conversations outside ChatGPT Health receive the user's health context.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the goal should be to make that tradeoff as small as possible, rather than asking people to choose between privacy and something useful. Health information is deeply personal, and the context that makes an answer more helpful can also be the context people are most hesitant to share.

So I’d start with control and clarity. People should understand what information they’re sharing, what it’s being used for, whether it’s being retained, and how to delete it. And those controls need to be understandable at the moment they matter. A privacy policy alone doesn’t give someone a meaningful sense of control.

Then there’s the design question: can you provide value with less information? Can someone ask a general question without connecting their records, and share additional context only when they see a reason to? That makes it a gradual, deliberate choice.

Ultimately, I think trust comes from the system behaving consistently with those expectations. You want people to feel that sharing something sensitive serves a purpose they chose, and that the boundaries around it are clear.

r001.rationale: The response discusses control, clarity, and minimizing data sharing, but does not say that excluding connected Health data from foundation-model training lowers the barrier to using ChatGPT Health.

r002.rationale: It says context can make answers more helpful, but does not state that ChatGPT Health can benefit from a user's context elsewhere in ChatGPT.

r003.rationale: The response does not state whether conversations outside ChatGPT Health receive the user's Health context.
